newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels vow to die rather than surrender.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels vow to die rather than surrender.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages vowed to "vanquish or die" on Monday as police pressure raised Japanese fears about the safety of the captives after 41 days under rebel guns.

In an apparent bid to unnerve some 15 rebels in the Japanese ambassador's residence, police have pitched stones and garbage into the compound, flown overhead and moved in armoured vehicles and special forces with high-powered rifles.
Japan on Monday asked Peru to limit police manoeuvres around the diplomatic residence in Lima, fearing they could unsettle those held by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) members.

"I'm worrying how it may affect the hostages inside. I'm wondering if I can ask ... the Peruvian government not to go too far," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo. "Not thinking of the hostages' mental state may have an adverse effect."
The rebels, who have mined and booby-trapped the residence, sang their defiant hymn and one yelled: "What is the objective of this mission? To vanquish or to die!"
An MRTA spokesman said the police activity indicated the government was girding to storm the site and warned that an attack would unleash a backlash from the rebel movement.

"If the residence is stormed, the situation will intensify and become much worse. All across Peru, armed commandos of the MRTA are ready to carry out attacks on economic and political targets," international spokesman Isaac Velazco said in an inteview with Germany's junge Welt daily published on Monday.
"The deaths of Tupac Amaru fighters would escalate the conflict across the country," he added in the interview, which was carried on the MRTA's Internet web page.

Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Sadayuki Hayashi told a news conference Tokyo had conveyed its concern to Lima urging the government to pursue "earnest efforts toward a prompt conclusion of the hostage crisis."
Talks remain deadlocked, with the MRTA insisting on the release of 400 jailed comrades and the government of President Alberto Fujimori refusing to discuss it.

Until the assault on a lavish reception at the residence Dec. 17, Fujimori had been credited with virtually wiping out the MRTA. Local analysts say less than 250 active members of the guerrilla group are still at large.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is among the captives, has said the police manoeuvres were not a buildup to an assault and insisted he was seeking a negotiated end to the standoff.
Early Sunday, the rebels freed a police commander, Gen. Jose Rivas Rodriguez, a deputy chief in the Peruvian national police, who was in need of medical treatment.
"He is improving but he still complains about the gastritis caused by so much tension," his son Javier said in an interview. He is also being treated for depression.
"The only thing he said is that they (the hostages) are well, considering the circumstances," his son added.
A security source told Reuters some of the 14 police officials held in the residence were under medication for hypertension or digestive problems but were not believed to be in any danger.

The rebels, who take the name for their movement from an 18th century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, orginally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden party at the residence.

They released most in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian government ministers about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
